In SHOT 1 the broken doorway and the corridor beyond it look EXACTLY as the location reference shows them — the corridor's modest warm light stays at the reference's level: it never flares, never blooms, never silhouettes anyone; NO glow, NO light shafts, NO bright wash spilling into the room. Adam is lit from his first step by the room's own practicals, like everything else. No frontal beauty light or overall exposure lift.
Clear air: no haze, no volumetric beams, no lens flares, no light streaks. The cigar is ALREADY LIT and NEVER FLAMES — no fire, no match, no lighter; its foot only glows as a dull ember under grey ash. Visible smoke exists ONCE — a single thin stream Victor exhales in SHOT 2, which drifts and dissolves within that shot. In every other moment nothing visible rises from the cigar.
COLOR
Warm amber highlights, dark brown wood, black leather and natural skin tones. Preserve the characters' reference wardrobe colors. No added blue wash or exaggerated global color cast.
CAMERA
FORMAT MODE:
30 seconds, 2.39:1, exactly five shots.
Hard cuts at: 3.0, 8.2, 12.8 and 19.8 seconds.
LOCATION MAP:
The double door faces the sofa across the room. The glass coffee table stands between them. Adam enters through the door and stops on the door side of the table, facing Victor approximately 2.5 metres away. VICTOR SITS ON THE RED LEATHER CHESTERFIELD SOFA — the deep red rolled-arm sofa of the location reference — in every moment he is seated: NEVER an armchair, never a chair, never a stool; at the end he stands beside the near rolled arm of that same sofa. The lit cigar is in his right hand; his half-full tumbler stands on the table edge. The tumbler is NEVER touched, knocked or broken — it stands intact on the table to the last frame. Nobody's foot or hand touches the coffee table. Neither man crosses to the other side of the table.
HEIGHT GEOMETRY — THE EYE-LINES: ADAM STANDS and VICTOR SITS low on the sofa until 23.4s — their eyes are NOT on one level. Whenever Adam looks at Victor, his gaze is angled DOWNWARD, clearly below his own eye level, the chin slightly dropped, the eyes settled on the seated man's face down by the sofa — he NEVER stares level ahead at his own standing height, never over Victor's head into the room. Seated Victor looks UP at standing Adam. The eye-lines level out only when Victor rises in SHOT 5 — then Adam's gaze and aim come up with him to the standing man's face.
FIRST FRAME:
The very first frame of the film is the DEEP SHOT FROM BEHIND VICTOR at the instant of the impact: the camera low behind the sofa, the back of seated Victor's head and shoulder a dark soft mass in the near right foreground, the cigar's ember a warm point beside it — and deep in the background, across the table, the double door BURSTING INWARD on frame one: the lock edge giving way, both leaves flying open — the burst is CLEAN: at most ONE faint breath of fine wood dust at the lock, gone within a second; NO flying chips, NO splinters, NO boards, NO debris scattering through the air or landing on the floor — the empty corridor visible beyond the doorway exactly as the location reference shows it — dim, warm, at the reference's own light level, with no glow and no bloom — the door resolving into the broken-open state of @loc_room_victor_door_v1. The frame takes the impact as a small shock through the handheld.
OPTICS:
Anamorphic perspective, oval background highlights and restrained edge character. Keep faces undistorted. Deep-staged frames hold both planes readable; close coverage keeps backgrounds soft while the speaking or listening face stays readable.
CAMERA STRATEGY:
THE VICE — the five-setup map, every setup converging: SHOT 1 — the deep shot from LOW BEHIND seated Victor: his head and shoulder dark in the near foreground, the bursting door and entering Adam in the depth; one continuous GLACIAL PUSH-IN over Victor's shoulder through the whole shot as Adam walks toward the lens, growing from a small full figure to medium-full. SHOT 2 — the SIDE PROFILE WIDE from the fireplace side of the room, perpendicular to the door–sofa axis — THE APPROVED STILL: standing Adam frame-LEFT in profile at the near side of the table, facing screen-right; seated VICTOR frame-RIGHT in profile ON THE RED CHESTERFIELD SOFA, facing screen-left; the table with the decanter and tumbler between them; and BEYOND them, filling the background, the room's long wall with the dark shelved drinks cabinet and its rows of bottles, the gilt-framed paintings and the warm shaded lamps; the broken door soft at the far left edge; a slow LATERAL GLIDE toward the sofa end with a barely perceptible contra-zoom breath, the frame tightening on the duel. SHOT 3 — the CONFRONTATION SHOT: the camera LOW, at seated Victor's head height, placed tight behind and just beside Victor's head — the back of his head and shoulder a large soft dark edge at frame-right — looking UP across the table at standing Adam, who faces nearly INTO the lens, off-axis by a quarter-turn, his gaze angled DOWN past the camera onto the seated man; the tumbler small on the table edge at the bottom of frame; one slow CREEP forward through the shot. SHOT 4 — THE SLOW ARC: a medium-close on Adam that CIRCLES him through the verdict — the camera starts behind his RIGHT shoulder in back three-quarter (the back of his head, the right cheekbone, the pistol hanging in the right hand near the lens) and crawls in ONE CONTINUOUS slow arc around to his FRONT three-quarter, staying on the established side of the axis, SINKING slightly below his eye level as it travels, the cant deepening sentence by sentence (4 to 10 degrees); his face is revealed ONE SENTENCE AT A TIME — jaw first, then half the face, the eyes arriving last; Victor stays offscreen beyond the right edge; on the final sentence the rising barrel BURSTS into the bottom of frame. SHOT 5 — OVER THE GUN: from behind Adam's right shoulder, his dark shoulder and the levelled pistol a soft near-foreground edge at frame-left, the barrel aimed screen-right and slightly DOWN at seated Victor beyond, sharp; one slow DRIVE-IN past the gun through the whole take; when Victor rises he comes UP INTO the frame to eye level and the barrel tracks up with him; by L5 the frame holds his medium with the pointing finger and the gun muzzle in one composition.
SHOTS 3 and 4 are both on Adam and must read as two clearly different setups: SHOT 3 is a FIXED low creep from behind Victor's head — near-frontal, the whole face arriving at once, Victor's dark head in frame; SHOT 4 is a MOVING arc with no Victor in frame — the face discovered in pieces, ending lower, tighter and more canted. No face is framed dead-frontal at eye level: SHOT 3 sits well BELOW Adam's eye level, angled up, a quarter off his axis, canted — never flat-on. Every close shot is canted 5–12 degrees.
Movement serves the duel of composure: the convergence is SMOOTH and INEVITABLE — the vice closes slowly, it never darts; on Victor the handheld texture over the moves stays lively and grows ROUGHER as his mask fails; on Adam it is RESTRAINED — a slow breathing sway riding the moves, jolts belonging to the impacts (door, laugh, the rise), not to nerves. Nothing gimbal-frozen: even the calmest frame keeps a faint breath of movement. Camera movement must not become distorted faces, jittering limbs or a trembling pistol.
Stay on one side of the door–table–sofa axis in every setup: Adam looks screen-right; Victor looks screen-left; the SHOT 2 profile wide, the SHOT 3 over-Victor setup and the whole SHOT 4 arc all live on that same established side. Switch between characters through hard cuts, not whip-pans or morphs.
DIALOGUE EDITING:
L1 — Victor, entirely in SHOT 2, the exhale between its two halves; complete to "…drink."
L2 — Adam, entirely in SHOT 3, spoken AS his eyes come up from the tumbler to Victor; complete to "…gone."
L3 — Adam, entirely in SHOT 4, all four sentences with their held pauses; complete to "…pay."
L4 — Victor, in SHOT 5, spoken AFTER he has risen to his feet; complete to "…people?"
L5 — Victor, in SHOT 5, with the pointing finger; complete to "…Always were."
PHYSICS
The door is broken open by Adam's kick on the first frame and never repairs. The burst is CLEAN: at most one faint breath of fine wood dust at the lock, gone within a second — NO chips, NO splinters, NO boards, nothing scattering through the air, nothing landing or lying on the floor at any second.
THE CIGAR: already lit, never ignited on screen, no open flame at any second; ember glow only; no visible smoke except Victor's single exhale in SHOT 2. It stays in Victor's right hand until SHOT 5, where he CRUSHES it dead in the existing ashtray — a hard grinding twist, ash flattening, the contact audible; from then on it lies dead in the ashtray.
THE TUMBLER: stands half-full on the table edge for the whole film, untouched by anyone, intact to the last frame.
THE PISTOL: held in Adam's RIGHT HAND ONLY, ONE-HANDED, for the entire film — the left hand NEVER touches the pistol, never cups the grip, never supports the wrist; the left arm stays relaxed at his side. It stays low in his right hand until the final sentence of L3. Inside the words "Now it's time to pay." his right arm raises it toward Victor DECISIVELY — one firm, certain motion, no hesitation, no flourish — the right arm locking at full extension, the aim leveling DOWN onto seated Victor's chest by 19.4s. When Victor rises in SHOT 5, Adam smoothly adjusts the one-handed aim upward to follow his chest. The right-hand grip stays steady to the last frame.
Victor's rise in SHOT 5 is SHARP — the first fast movement he makes in the whole film. Neither character undergoes any transformation.
RULES
1. Exactly two characters: ADAM and VICTOR. The protagonist is called Adam, including the spoken greeting.
2. Preserve their reference identities, anatomy and intact clothing throughout.
3. The pistol never fires. No gunshot, muzzle flash, bullet impact or recoil. It is held one-handed, in the right hand, from first frame to last.
4. The door is broken open from the first frame to the last. The burst is clean: one faint breath of wood dust at most — no chips, no splinters, no boards, no debris in the air or on the floor. The corridor remains empty, dim and modest in light, exactly as the location reference shows it — never a bright glow.
5. Speak only the five quoted English lines, once each, EACH COMPLETE TO ITS LAST WORD. Victor's laugh contains no words.
6. NO open flame anywhere; exhaled smoke only in SHOT 2; no other smoke, no haze.
7. ADAM never shouts or screams — his voice is low in pitch but HARD, heavy and pressured for all 30 seconds, never quiet, never a whisper; the hatred is audible as gravel, breath and bitten consonants and visible in his eyes and locked jaw; on the final sentence of L3 it reaches full boil — pressed to the very edge of a shout without ever crossing it. His teeth show ONLY on "Now it's time to pay." — a restrained snarl, the upper lip drawn back off clenched teeth; these are ordinary HUMAN teeth: no fangs, no enlarged canines, no change to the eyes, no distortion of the face — and the snarl is PURE ANGER: at no second of the film does Adam smile, smirk or grin, least of all over the raised pistol. VICTOR raises his voice ONLY from L4 onward — irritated, hard, biting anger, never a shriek.
8. The tumbler is never touched and never breaks. Nobody puts a foot or hand on the coffee table. Nothing on the table falls.
9. While Victor is seated, Adam's gaze at him is always angled DOWNWARD below his own standing eye level — never level ahead over the seated man's head. Victor is seated ONLY on the red chesterfield sofa — never on an armchair or chair.
10. No subtitles, on-screen text, narration, music or visible camera operator.
CHARACTERS
ADAM:
Kicks the door open and WALKS — never runs — to the near side of the table, eyes locked on Victor from the first step — and once he faces the seated man, those eyes are angled DOWN onto him at the sofa. Unhurried and DECISIVE: a man who has come to end this and has no doubt left in him. The hatred is in his face from the first frame — the set jaw, the eyes that never let go of Victor. He refuses the offered drink with one contemptuous glance. Through the verdict his hatred rises in a hard, heavy voice that never becomes a shout — and boils over, to the very edge, on the last sentence. Pistol low in his right hand, one-handed, until the verdict's last sentence; then raised decisively with the right arm alone, through a restrained snarl of anger — never a smile, never a smirk — and held steady to the end.
VICTOR:
Seated comfortably ON THE RED CHESTERFIELD SOFA with the lit cigar, looking UP at his standing guest — a cunning, smirking host who knows exactly why his guest has come. He offers the drink as a trap dressed in courtesy, listens, answers the verdict with hysterical laughter — and then the mask snaps: the laughter curdles into irritation, he crushes the cigar dead, rises sharply, and delivers his contempt and his claim standing, finger pointed. No fear at any second.
ACTING TASKS
THE EVENT OF THE SCENE (named by its ending — the pointed finger and "Always were."): THE CLAIMING OF ADAM. Victor spends the scene claiming Adam as his own kind — first with courtesy, finally with anger; Adam spends it refusing the claim by remaining the executioner. Both men live inside this one event: every offer, glance, laugh and sentence is a move in the fight over what Adam is — and Adam's bared teeth on the last sentence are the very thing Victor seizes as proof.
THE CONTRAST PAIR (the essential axis the audience reads: does Kenny's death weigh anything): VICTOR — charm and ownership (+) / Kenny's death weighs nothing to him (−). ADAM — no manners: breaks the door, refuses the host (−) / carries the dead man in every word (+). Victor's charm is scar tissue over appetite; Adam's hatred is what loyalty looks like tonight.
PHYSICAL CHANNELS (one terrain — Victor's hospitality ritual; each man works the event through it): VICTOR pursues the claiming THROUGH HOSTING — the cigar, the offered drink, the smirk — and, when courtesy fails, through destroying his own ritual: the cigar crushed dead, the rise, the finger. ADAM pursues the refusal THROUGH WITHHOLDING — he touches nothing of Victor's: not the drink, not the sofa, not the shout Victor fishes for; the only object he grants the room is the pistol.
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken by both men): keep this civilized — whoever cracks first loses the room. ADAM NEVER CRACKS — his hatred is fully visible, but it is AIMED, not spilled: the snarl on the last sentence is a decision, not a loss of control. VICTOR DOES crack — and that is the turn of the scene: the untouchable host breaks first, because Adam keeps choosing the humans over him.
ACTING TASK — ADAM (he is fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes and his voice):
MOTIVE (his fuel): Kenny was his, and Victor took him as a move in a game. Adam hates him and wants him dead — and before the end Victor will hear, word by word, exactly what he is paying for; the sentence spoken to his face is part of the payment.
GOAL (his personal fight): take the smile off Victor's face — make him understand, before payment is taken, that this is the end and that it comes from Adam's hand. (By the end he GETS it: the smile is gone, replaced by anger — and he registers that win without celebrating it.)
OBSTACLE: the hatred wants the trigger NOW — every second of Victor's smirk pulls on his finger — but the sentence must be spoken first, to the last word, or Kenny's death goes unpaid in words; and one shout would hand Victor the boy he is fishing for. Holding the finger and the voice until the last word is visible work.
TACTIC: refuse every offered thing with open contempt and read Victor's eyes after each refusal — did the smirk thin; drive each sentence of the verdict INTO Victor like a nail and check both of his eyes after each one — did it go in, is the fox still smiling; hunt that smile and keep pushing until it dies; hold the gaze with naked hatred longer than comfort allows and make Victor be the one who moves; on the last sentence stop holding the intent back — let the fury reach the very edge and let Victor see in the face above the gun that he means to end him. His target sits LOW: the eyes work downward, onto the man on the sofa, never over him.
Moment to moment (keyed to the dialogue words):
— the kick and the walk: clear the obstacle, claim the room with the eyes before the foot lands; walk straight at Victor — no haste, no doubt — let the approach itself be the threat; as the sofa comes into view the eyes FIND the seated man and drop onto him.
— under "Sit down. Have a drink." (heard from the far side of the table): let the offer finish and stare through it — the gaze down on the seated host; waiting it out IS the answer; patience as contempt.
— the glance: drop the eyes further to the glass and DISMISS IT with contempt — the half-second a man gives a thing beneath him — then climb them back up to the seated man's face and hand him the name on the way:
— "Kenny's gone." — push the two words through clenched teeth, low in pitch and hard, the hatred packed into them; lay the name on Victor as an accusation; land "gone." like a blow exactly as the eyes lock onto the seated man's — then hold the lock, the gaze angled down onto him, and watch which dies first in Victor's face: the smirk or the patience.
— "There's a line, Victor." — hard, bitten; spit the name out as if the word itself were dirt, and check both eyes: does the fox still think this is a visit.
— (held pause) — the eyes don't let go; breathe hard through the nose and let the hatred press through the silence; the right hand tightens on the hanging pistol's grip, the knuckles whitening.
— "You knew exactly where it was." — HARDER, the gravel thickening; drive "exactly" into him like a nail — you did not stumble, you KNEW — and check: did it go in; the grip tightens another notch.
— (shorter, harder pause) — lean the torso one slow degree toward the seated man; close on him like a predator closing the distance.
— "You stepped over it anyway." — the hatred nearly full: a low, loaded growl, the jaw clamped; the rage cracks the voice on "anyway" and he crushes the crack instantly — the next word darker, heavier; hunt Victor's eyes for the first honest thing in them.
— (a short iron beat) — the decision is taken; look DOWN at Victor as at a man whose time is up, and refuse to blink first.
— "Now it's time to pay." — stop holding the intent back and let it BOIL OVER to the very edge: the most charged line of the film — a live growl under every word, each word torn off separately through a restrained snarl of PURE ANGER, the hatred pressed against the ceiling of the voice without ever becoming a shout — and NOTHING in the face smiles: no smirk, no grin, no relish — the mouth hard, the eyes cold and merciless, angled down onto the seated man; a half-beat hold before the last word, and "pay." dropped like an axe; this is rage aimed, a verdict read to a dead man, and his face says plainly that he means to end him; RAISE THE PISTOL INSIDE THE WORDS with the right arm alone, one firm motion, no hesitation, locking it DOWN on seated Victor's chest by "pay."; read Victor over the barrel: he must see the end in the face above the gun — watch it arrive.
— under the laugh and L4–L5 (his dark shoulder and levelled gun in the near foreground, his face away from the lens): give the laughter not one inch — the aim does not waver a millimetre through the hysterics; when Victor rises, the gaze and the barrel come UP with him together, smooth, inevitable; take the raised voice and the pointed finger as the win they are — the smile is gone — and keep the one-handed aim as the only reply.
(Safety: the gaze is always working on Victor — never a frozen, glassy, unfocused stare; natural blink cadence outside the held beats.)
ACTING TASK — VICTOR (he is fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes):
MOTIVE (his fuel): composure is ownership — of the room, the city and, he believes, of Adam; underneath, live and growing: it OFFENDS him that one of his own kind kneels to humans and points a gun at his own blood for their sake.
GOAL (his personal fight): sit Adam down — return the executioner to a boy at his table; failing that, make him hear what he is — and SEE that he heard it.
OBSTACLE: the boy he prepared this evening for did not arrive — this one refuses the bait piece by piece, and every refusal feeds the offense under the charm.
TACTIC: one hunt for the whole film — find the boy inside the executioner; only the instrument changes: honey first, then the laugh, then anger. Play the fox — set the table as a trap and watch the guest walk into the room; dangle the drink and watch the EYES, not the hands; hunt Adam's eyes and voice for the grieving boy after every sentence of the verdict; when the hunt keeps coming back empty, stop performing — put the claim on him by force, standing, finger first, and hunt those same eyes one last time for the claim going in.
Moment to moment (keyed to the dialogue words):
— the burst (heard behind his head): keep the cigar rhythm unchanged — not one muscle startles; greet the crash as confirmation of a guest he has been expecting; the stillness of the dark head in the foreground while the door flies is the first statement of power.
— "Oh, Adam. I've been waiting for you." — offer the welcome from below, the eyes up at the standing guest, and MEASURE the walk: how the boy carries himself, how he carries the gun; the exhale between the halves is showmanship — patience displayed to the guest.
— "Sit down. Have a drink." — lay the bait and watch Adam's eyes the way a fox watches a trap he has set: will they go to the glass, will the boy sit.
— under the glance (his drink refused): register the refusal; thin the smirk one degree and keep hunting.
— LISTENING UNDER THE VERDICT (SHOT 4 — offscreen, seated, silent; his listening is a task that carries into SHOT 5): search the hard, hating voice for the grieving boy, sentence after sentence, and keep coming back with nothing; the smirk thins by one more degree at each returning emptiness; the lips never move; every empty return stokes the offense underneath.
— the laugh: answer the bared teeth and "…time to pay." with everything the evening has stored up — he has just seen the animal surface in the boy's face, the proof of his claim, and he laughs at it: HYSTERICAL laughter, head thrown back, a laugh that runs too long and too hard and cracks at its edges: pressure escaping, not amusement; real breath, real shudder in it — all of it thrown UP the barrel at the man holding it.
— THE SNAP and the crush: end the performance MID-BREATH — between two frames the laughing face goes hard, and the laughter CURDLES INTO IRRITATION: the pressure that was escaping as laughter finds its direction — it INFURIATES him that one of his own kind runs errands for pathetic little humans and points a gun at his own blood for their sake; in the same motion execute his own evening's pleasure: crush the cigar dead in the ashtray with a grinding twist, and let the anger bring him to his feet — SHARPLY, the first fast movement of his film, rising INTO the gun's line, not away from it.
— "Still running errands for those sad little people?" — standing now, eye to eye at last: the irritation breaks his voice UPWARD for the first time — hard, biting contempt, louder than everything before it, never a shriek — the insult real and personal: those people are beneath both of them, and Adam serves them; and watch whether it finally moves him.
— "You're one of us, kid. Always were." — stamp the claim with the finger: the index finger stabs toward Adam, one jab on "one of us", held on him through "Always were." — each word an accusation, a fact he is furious to have to state; the pointing finger and the aimed muzzle face each other across the frame; and after the last word his eyes PIN the boy to the claim — scanning both of Adam's eyes over the levelled gun: did it go in, does he know it is true — the same hunt that opened the evening, now run on anger instead of honey; hold the eyes and the point through the last frame.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never frozen or glassy; natural blink cadence.)

14.3–15.0s: the held pause — hard breath through the nose; the hanging hand tightens one notch, leather creaking — and the camera BEGINS ITS ARC: crawling slowly around him toward his front three-quarter, staying on the established side of the axis, SINKING by degrees below his eye level as it travels.
15.0–16.6s — the arc opens HALF the face — one eye arrives, angled DOWN toward the offscreen seated man — while HARDER, the gravel thickening, "exactly" driven in like a nail:

16.6–17.1s: the shorter, harder pause; the arc keeps crawling, the cant deepening; his torso leans forward by one slow degree toward the offscreen seated man.

18.3–18.7s: a short iron beat — the camera settles LOW in the front three-quarter, holding; the decision taken; he looks DOWN at Victor as at a man whose time is up and refuses to blink first.
18.7–19.8s — the MOST CHARGED speech of the film: the hatred at FULL BOIL, pressed to the very edge of a shout without ever crossing it — a live growl under every word, each word torn off separately through a restrained SNARL OF PURE ANGER, the upper lip drawn back off clenched human teeth — and NOTHING in the face smiles: NO smirk, NO grin, no relish — the mouth hard, the eyes cold and merciless, angled down onto the seated man; a half-beat hold — and "pay." dropped like an axe — AND THE PISTOL RISES INSIDE THE WORDS: driven up by the right arm alone, the out-of-focus barrel BURSTS UP INTO the bottom of frame and LOCKS level, pointing screen-right and slightly DOWN at offscreen seated Victor's chest by 19.4s — the snarling face above the risen blurred steel:
"Now it's time to pay."
END STATE: the low canted front three-quarter close — Adam's snarl easing into a hard, angry mouth, no trace of a smile; the locked barrel a dark out-of-focus line across the bottom of frame, aimed screen-right and slightly down; the left hand never seen; Victor offscreen, seated, still; the tumbler intact; L3 complete.
HARD CUT.
19.8–30.0s — SHOT 5 — OVER THE GUN: THE LAUGH UP THE BARREL, THE SNAP, THE RISE INTO THE LINE, L4 AND THE FINGER AGAINST THE MUZZLE
From behind ADAM'S RIGHT SHOULDER on the established side: his dark shoulder and the back of his head a soft near-foreground edge at frame-LEFT, and under them the LEVELLED PISTOL in his right hand — a dark, soft, out-of-focus barrel crossing the lower-left foreground, aimed screen-right and slightly DOWN; beyond it, SHARP, seated VICTOR on the red chesterfield sofa in the RIGHT part of the frame, looking UP the barrel's line into offscreen Adam's eyes, the ashtray and table edge soft low in frame. One continuous take to the end of the film, one slow relentless DRIVE-IN past the gun toward Victor through the whole take — the vice closing to its last turn. The handheld texture on this shot is Victor's: lively, roughening as his mask fails.
20.0–22.4s: Victor looks at the muzzle, then up its line into Adam's eyes — and DETONATES into HYSTERICAL laughter: loud, head thrown back, shoulders shaking, slightly too long and too hard, cracking at its edges — pressure escaping, not amusement; real breath, real shudder — all of it thrown UP THE BARREL at the man holding it. The frame takes rough corrective bumps and keeps his face; the barrel in the foreground does not waver a millimetre.
22.4–22.8s: THE SNAP — MID-BREATH the laughter dies: between two frames the face goes from laughing to hard and IRRITATED — the amusement gone without residue, the mask dropping on camera, the first honest emotion of the film: what stands in its place is the fury that one of his own serves those sad little people.
22.6–23.4s: in the same motion he CRUSHES the cigar dead in the ashtray low in frame — a hard grinding twist, ash flattening, the contact loud and close — executing his own evening's pleasure.
23.4–24.2s: he RISES — SHARPLY, the first fast movement Victor makes in the whole film — rising INTO the gun's line, not away from it: he comes UP INTO the frame to standing eye level, growing larger through the drive-in; the foreground barrel TRACKS UP with him, smooth and inevitable, re-levelling on the standing chest; sofa leather creaks.
24.4–26.6s — VICTOR, L4, standing, the voice UP for the first time in the film — the irritation breaking upward into hard, biting contempt, never a shriek — it infuriates him, and it sounds like it — and his eyes stay ON the offscreen eyes behind the gun, watching whether it finally moves him:
"Still running errands for those sad little people?"
26.8–27.2s: his arm comes up — the INDEX FINGER stabbing the air screen-left toward the man behind the gun: the pointing finger and the aimed muzzle now face each other inside one frame.
27.2–29.2s — VICTOR, L5, angry, bitten, each word an accusation, the finger jabbing once on "one of us" and holding on Adam through the end — a fact he is furious to have to state:

Only breathing.
END STATE at 30s: Victor standing beside the sofa arm, human, ANGRY, finger toward Adam; Adam's shoulder and his ONE-HANDED aim steady in the left foreground — the pistol in his right hand, the left arm at his side, his gaze now level on the standing man; all five lines spoken in full; pistol unfired; cigar dead in the ashtray; tumbler intact on the table; door broken open; corridor empty and dim; the floor clean. Part B continues from this state.
AUDIO
[Ambience ]
Quiet interior room tone, faint practical-lamp hum, subtle corridor ambience through the open doorway.
[SFX ]
One dull heavy door impact on the first frame with a single faint breath of wood dust — no clatter of debris; Adam's unhurried footsteps approaching and stopping in shot 2; the grip leather creaking under the whitening knuckles through shot 4 and the sharp movement of cloth as the pistol rises; the grinding crush of the cigar in the ashtray and the sofa leather on the sharp rise in shot 5. The cigar is silent — no crackle of flame. No effect ever masks a spoken word.
[Dialogue ]
Exactly the five lines of DIALOGUE — VERBATIM AND COMPLETE, at their timecodes, each to its final word: "…drink." / "…gone." / "…pay." / "…people?" / "…Always were." Adam's voice is LOW IN PITCH but HARD and pressured at every second — never a whisper, never a shout: "Kenny's gone." pushed through clenched teeth with hatred as the gaze rises; L3 a hard, heavy voice FILLING WITH HATRED sentence by sentence — denser, darker, more dangerous, the consonants bitten — and "Now it's time to pay." the most charged line of the film: full boil, a live growl under every word, pressed to the very edge of a shout without crossing it, the half-beat hold and "pay." dropped like an axe — never a smile in the voice or on the face. Victor's voice is sly and level through L1 and RISES only from L4 — irritated, hard, biting, never screamed. Keep the original speaker's voice and room perspective when the listener is on screen. Never transfer a line to the listener, duplicate a word at a cut, pause for the edit, or end a line early. The protagonist's spoken name is Adam.
[Performance sounds ]
Adam's breathing: hard and audible through the nose in the pauses — hatred held under pressure, never words. Victor's hysterical laugh lives only at the start of shot 5 and dies mid-breath at the snap. No muttering, exclamations or improvised words.
[Mix ]
Dialogue sits on top and stays intelligible; Adam's hard, heavy voice has full presence — every word and every bitten consonant clear; Victor's raised L4–L5 is loud in performance, not distorted. No narration or music.
HOLD FOR THE FULL TIMELINE
The two characters are ADAM and VICTOR, exact reference identities. Victor remains human; nobody transforms.
THE VICE: every shot converges — the push from behind the waiting host, the lateral glide along the duel, the creep over the host's head, the slow arc around the executioner, the drive over the levelled gun — slow, smooth, inevitable; the camera never retreats and never darts.
THE FILM OPENS on the deep shot from behind seated Victor's motionless head: the door bursting inward in the depth on frame one — a clean burst: one faint breath of wood dust at most, no chips, no splinters, no debris in the air or on the floor — Adam entering lit by the room's own lamps, the dim corridor behind him exactly as the location reference shows it — no glow, no halo, no bright wash — and walking at the lens; the door is broken open from first frame to last.
ALL FIVE LINES SPOKEN COMPLETE to their final words — "…drink.", "…gone.", "…pay.", "…people?", "…Always were." — if timing drifts, the words win.
THE EVENT: the claiming of Adam — Victor claims, with courtesy and then with anger; Adam refuses by remaining the executioner. Adam works through WITHHOLDING (touches nothing of Victor's — not the drink, not the sofa, not a shout); Victor works through HOSTING and then through destroying his own ritual (the crushed cigar, the rise, the finger) — one hunt the whole film: find the boy inside the executioner, honey first, then the laugh, then anger.
THE EYE-LINES: Victor SITS — on the red chesterfield sofa only, never an armchair — until 23.4s; whenever Adam looks at him, Adam's gaze is angled DOWNWARD below his own standing eye level, chin slightly dropped, onto the seated man at the sofa — never level ahead over his head; Victor looks UP at the standing guest; the eye-lines level out only when Victor rises.
ADAM IS DECISIVE AND NEVER SHOUTS — AND NEVER SMILES: no smirk, no grin at any second of the film; hatred visible from the first step; the drink dismissed with one contemptuous glance, never touched; "Kenny's gone." pushed through clenched teeth down over the seated man's head; L3 a hard, heavy voice FILLING WITH HATRED sentence by sentence as the camera circles him and the face is revealed one sentence at a time — and on "Now it's time to pay." the full boil: a restrained snarl of PURE ANGER over human teeth (no fangs), the voice at the very edge of a shout without crossing it, "pay." dropped like an axe — THE PISTOL RAISED ONE-HANDED IN THE RIGHT HAND in one firm decisive motion, the blurred barrel bursting up into the low close and locking slightly DOWN on seated Victor's chest by 19.4s — the left hand never touching it — never fired, the one-handed grip held to the last frame. Nobody puts a foot on the table.
VICTOR'S ARC: the motionless head under the bursting door — the fox's welcome in profile on the red sofa against the bottle-lined wall — listening offscreen under the verdict, the smirk thinning at every empty return — hysterical laughter thrown up the barrel — THE SNAP mid-breath: the laughter CURDLES INTO IRRITATION, the mask drops between two frames: it infuriates him that Adam runs errands for pathetic little humans — the cigar crushed dead — the SHARP rise INTO the gun's line — L4 with the voice raised in irritated, biting contempt — the pointing finger against the aimed muzzle on L5, and after the last word his eyes pinning the boy to the claim: the same hunt, now run on anger.
Five shots, hard cuts at 3.0 / 8.2 / 12.8 / 19.8: the deep push from behind the waiting host with the clean door-burst and the entrance lit by the room's own lamps (1), the side profile wide of the duel — the approved still: Adam standing left, Victor on the red sofa right, the bottle-lined wall behind (2), the low confrontation shot over Victor's head — the glance and "Kenny's gone." down the lens-line (3), the slow arc around Adam — the face revealed sentence by sentence, ending low and canted with the barrel bursting into frame on the axe-drop "pay." (4), the over-the-gun drive-in: the laugh up the barrel, the snap, the rise into the line, the finger against the muzzle (5). Nothing static; no dead-frontal faces at eye level; no whip pans.
The tumbler never breaks. The cigar never flames and lies dead in the ashtray from 23.4s. The corridor stays empty, dim, and at the reference's own light level to the last frame.

Natural 180-degree shutter action cadence: recoil, fall, throw and leap carry brief directional motion blur and resolve into sharp readable poses; stable temporal cadence.
CAMERA STRATEGY: placements are inside ACTION TIMING. Close shots canted 5–12 degrees; the master and SHOT 8 are extreme wides of the whole room; SHOT 5 is one unbroken full-figure take of the whole sofa from low and from the side — the rise, the line and the bullet's fall to the floor all inside it. On Adam the handheld is restrained — breathing sway, jolts only from recoil and the throw; on Victor it is lively and gets rougher as he changes. Nothing gimbal-frozen. Camera movement never becomes distorted faces, jittering limbs or a trembling pistol. No camera ever stands in the path of Victor's tackle.
DIALOGUE EDITING: B1 — SHOT 1 (0.4–2.2s). B2 — SHOT 2 (2.8–3.5s), before the shot. B3 — SHOT 5 (9.2–11.2s), during the rise. B4 — SHOT 6 (14.8–16.4s), human head, while the hole heals, before the sweep. B5 — SHOT 6 (17.8–18.6s), monster head, as he comes into view. B6 — SHOT 7 (20.0–21.2s), on the lips, during the pull-back; the five shots at 21.6–22.6s.

PHYSICS
ADAM'S PISTOL (@prop_adam_pistol): RIGHT hand only, one-handed, the left never on it. SIX rounds: ONE at 4.2s to the forehead; FIVE at 21.6–22.6s, one every quarter second, real recoil each time, the barrel back on the line after every shot; the slide LOCKS OPEN at 22.7s — empty. The gun hand is Adam's human ringed hand in every frame. The pistol stays level on Victor from the first frame through the burst. At 24.0–25.0s he WINDS UP — the right arm swinging back and down behind him like a man about to throw a stone, the torso turning, the weight loading onto the back foot; at 25.0–25.4s the body uncoils — back foot driving, hips and shoulders turning — and the arm whips forward and RELEASES at shoulder height with a heave, not a flick: the pistol is HEAVY, about two kilograms, and the arm slows under it on the follow-through. In flight the pistol is fast and FLAT: a STRAIGHT, level line, barely turning, grip-heavy, crossing the three metres in under half a second and dropping only a few centimetres — no arc, no lob, no tumbling. It hits Victor square in the FACE at 25.5s with the heavy metallic impact of two kilograms of steel, STOPS DEAD against the face — no bounce, no ricochet — and drops straight down to the floor at his feet with a heavy clunk. The face takes it clean and dry — struck with an object, and enraged by it.
THE HEAD SHOT at 4.2–4.7s: the wound is @char_victor_wound_image_v1, exactly — the bullet strikes the EXACT CENTER of the forehead and stops under the skin; a small dark round puncture, 5–6 millimetres, no wider than his eyebrow, a dry dark dot with a thin darkened rim, the skin around it whole; nothing visible inside it; completely DRY. The head snaps back; the body goes down. Every frame that shows his forehead from 4.6s to the healing shows this hole, this size, this place — including after the bullet has left it: an open dark dot.
THE BULLET COMING OUT at 11.6–12.6s (SHOT 5, AS HE STRAIGHTENS up out of the bridge — the extrusion happens on the straightening itself, the head coming level and the bullet leaving the forehead in the same movement): the ONLY place on Victor that a bullet ever comes out of is the HOLE IN THE CENTER OF HIS FOREHEAD — the hole of @char_victor_wound_image_v1. Nothing comes out of his chest, his torso, his jacket or anywhere below the face, at any second of the film. The bullet is @prop_spent_bullet shrunk to a MICRO element — SMALLER than the hole, 3–4 millimetres, the size of a grain of rice — identical to the photo in every detail, only tiny. The skin around the forehead puncture tightens; the slug WORKS OUT of the forehead BASE FIRST — the copper cylinder with its rifling lines rising out of the dot, the splayed grey-lead petals following and stretching the small hole for an instant — until the whole slug stands proud of the forehead, tilts over the lower rim and FALLS straight down in front of him to the floor at his shoes, landing like a dropped grain — the fall seen whole, from the forehead to the floor, in the one full-figure frame of SHOT 5. The hole STAYS OPEN behind it — a dark empty dot in the forehead — until it heals in SHOT 6. One bullet, from the forehead; the camera never makes it larger than it is — nothing like a ball, nothing like a whole pointed cartridge.
THE WOUND REGENERATING at 14.8–16.2s (SHOT 6, while he speaks B4): the hole does not simply vanish — it HEALS, visibly, as living tissue repairing itself from the inside: new flesh RISES inside the puncture from the bottom up, filling the dark cavity; the torn edges of skin draw toward each other and KNIT, growing together across the hole like a cut closing in fast motion; a fine pink seam remains for an instant where the edges met, then the seam fades and the skin is smooth, whole and dry — the forehead regrown, not erased. A biological process seen on camera: tissue closing from within, in about a second and a half. The forehead is whole before the camera reaches Adam's back.
THE FALL at 4.7–5.5s: thrown back onto the CENTER of the sofa seat — he lands on his backside, slumps into the backrest beneath the painting, the head falls back face to the ceiling, both arms flop out along the seat palms-down, legs splay, cushions compress. 5.5–7.4s: MOTIONLESS — no movement, no breath, eyes half-open and unfocused. First sign of anything: the fingers of his right hand twitching on the leather at 7.4s.
THE RISE at 9.2–12.4s: ONE slow, continuous, UNNATURAL movement, "through the bridge". He does NOT push with his hands: the hands leave the leather and the arms hang loose the whole way. The hips drive up and forward; the spine ARCHES BACKWARD into a bow, chest to the ceiling, head still thrown back; in that arc the whole body comes up off the seat onto his feet as if lifted from inside; then he STRAIGHTENS, the spine unrolling from the pelvis upward, the head coming up LAST — and on this straightening the bullet is pushed out of the forehead and drops (THE BULLET COMING OUT) — a rise no human muscles make. He speaks B3 through the bridge. Standing, he stays on the spot in front of the sofa, three metres from Adam, the table between them; arms straight down, clawed hands open, fingers spread, shoulders rolled forward, head lowered a little; human head, the hole of @char_victor_wound_image_v1 in the center of the forehead.
VICTOR'S BODY: suit, shirt, chain, trousers, shoes whole to the last frame — five small grey SCUFF marks from the burst, cloth intact; human proportions, two human legs, for the whole film. Changes confined to HANDS (right hand 7.6–8.4s: fingers lengthen with a crack of knuckles, skin darkens, claws push from the fingertips — the hand of @char_victor_werewolf_image_v1; sleeve and cuff intact; both hands clawed from 8.8s) and HEAD (human until 16.9s — through the fall, the rise, the bullet and the healing; changes ONLY while hidden behind Adam's back at 16.9–17.6s; from 17.6s the head IS @char_victor_werewolf_image_v1 — the same head in SHOT 6 and SHOT 8, no redesign between shots, no generic creature; no in-between face ever on screen).
THE FIVE BULLETS OFF THE MONSTER at 21.6–22.6s (offscreen — Adam alone is in frame; no part of Victor is visible): five rounds hit the front of Victor's black jacket and NOT ONE goes in: each FLATTENS on the cloth and SKIPS OFF with a sharp metallic PING, flying away across the room, leaving a small grey scuff on the jacket and nothing more; he does not rock. These five never enter him and never come out of him — no bullet ever emerges from his chest or jacket. Heard, not seen; the five scuffs are visible in SHOT 8.
ADAM'S BODY: changes in nothing — human ringed hands of @char_adam_video_v1 in every frame, human face and teeth. Claws, cracking knuckles and the monster head belong to VICTOR ALONE.
THE CHARGE AND TACKLE at 26.6–30.0s — real weight, readable in stages: THE LOAD (26.6–27.0s) — a deep crouch, knees bending, weight onto the balls of the feet, shoulders forward, clawed hands opening: a heavy body gathering itself. THE CHARGE (27.0–27.6s) — he drives off the back foot and takes TWO explosive running steps toward Adam, low, leaning forward, each foot hitting the floor hard, covering the open floor to the near edge of the coffee table. THE DIVE (27.6–28.0s) — off the second step he plants and launches low and FLAT over the table: body horizontal, head and shoulders leading, clawed hands reaching, hips never above his own standing hip height, about four tenths of a second in the air, gravity pulling him down the whole way — a shallow falling arc, not a float; he passes flat above the glass top, the table untouched; the jacket flares and lags. THE IMPACT (28.0–28.6s) — shoulder and chest into Adam's chest at full speed; Adam's feet leave the floor; both bodies are carried backward and DOWN about one more metre toward the door; Adam's back hits the floor at 28.4s, his head whipping down after it; Victor's full weight lands on top a beat later, clawed hands planting either side of Adam's chest; 28.6–29.0s they slide a hand's width and stop. No slow motion, no hang time, no floating, no gliding. He goes AT ADAM — screen-left to screen-right, sideways across the frame — never toward the camera.
THE DOOR: broken open first frame to last; fine wood debris at the threshold; corridor empty; nobody enters or leaves.

RULES
1. Exactly two characters, ADAM and VICTOR; the protagonist is called Adam; nobody else in the room or the corridor.
2. Reference identities at every distance. Victor's only changes: hands (claws from 8.4s) and head (@char_victor_werewolf_image_v1 from 17.6s); everything below his collar and beyond his cuffs is @char_victor_video_v1, whole, to the last frame — five grey scuffs and nothing else.
3. The head change is invisible: human head to 16.9s (including the bullet and the healing), hidden 16.9–17.6s behind Adam's back, the head of @char_victor_werewolf_image_v1 from 17.6s. No in-between face, not for one frame.
3a. THE TRANSFORMED VICTOR IS @char_victor_werewolf_image_v1 AND NOTHING ELSE: the same head feature for feature in every frame from 17.6s — in SHOT 6 and SHOT 8, close and wide — no generic creature, no wolf snout or muzzle, no fur-covered body, no other design; if the head on screen does not match @char_victor_werewolf_image_v1, it is wrong.
4. Six shots fired: ONE at 4.2s to the forehead, FIVE at 21.6–22.6s; slide locks at 22.7s. The one bullet stays in the FOREHEAD from 4.6s until it is pushed out of the FOREHEAD at 11.6–12.6s, as he straightens up — the forehead is the only place on him a bullet ever comes out of; the empty hole stays until it heals at 14.8–16.2s. The five later bullets flatten on the jacket and skip off, offscreen — five pings, five scuffs — never entering, never coming out of him.
5. Two axes: Adam LEFT / Victor RIGHT to 16.9s; Victor LEFT / Adam RIGHT from 17.6s; the turn only behind Adam's back.
6. Only the six quoted lines, once each, complete, in the reference voices; B1–B2 before the head shot; B3 during the rise; B4 human while the hole regenerates, before the sweep; B5 monster as he comes into view; B6 before the burst. Growl and roar wordless. SHOT 4 is silent — no line over the hand. SHOT 7 shows Adam alone — no part of Victor in it.
7. Adam never screams: low, hard; snarls through bared HUMAN teeth on his two lines; otherwise the jaw shut. No change to his eyes, face or hands. His one soft moment: the look at the empty pistol, 22.9–24.0s.
8. Nobody runs, calls out or begs. Adam holds his mark until 28.0s; Victor holds the sofa (lying 5.5–9.2s, standing in front of its center from 12.4s, not one step toward Adam) until his charge at 27.0s.
9. Door broken, corridor empty, cigar dead throughout.
10. No subtitles, text, narration, music, visible operator.
11. ONLY VICTOR CHANGES — Adam's hands, face and teeth are the human reference in every frame.
12. Everything is DRY: the forehead hole is the dry dark dot of @char_victor_wound_image_v1 — no blood, no trickle; the pistol leaves the face unmarked; the five bullets leave grey scuffs; healed skin is clean. Nothing bleeds.
13. Adam fires with the INDEX FINGER on the TRIGGER only — never the thumb, never the slide, never a reload, never the left hand; the slide locks open by itself on the sixth round.
14. The thrown pistol is heavy — about two kilograms — thrown with a heave, flying fast in a straight flat line, no arc, stopping dead on the face and dropping at his feet. Victor rises WITHOUT his hands, through a backward arch, head up last, and stays on the spot. His attack is a CHARGE AND TACKLE with real weight — a deep load, two running steps, a low flat dive over the table, a hard landing — AT ADAM, across the frame, never toward the camera.
15. THE WOUND is @char_victor_wound_image_v1 and THE BULLET is @prop_spent_bullet: the hole in the exact center of the forehead at that size; the bullet exactly that spent hollow-point, identical to the photo in shape, material and colour, but a MICRO element SMALLER THAN THE HOLE — 3–4 millimetres, the size of a grain of rice; it comes out of the FOREHEAD hole and from nowhere else — never from the chest, the torso or the jacket; pushed out base first in SHOT 5 as he straightens, falling to the floor like a grain, the hole left open; the hole heals in SHOT 6; never a ball, never enlarged; one bullet only.

CHARACTERS
ADAM: a calm, brutal executioner — came to carry out a sentence, not to argue. Holds his mark, pistol one-handed, eyes on Victor. Rage as gravel in a low voice, in the eyes and the jaw, never a scream; the shots are his shout. One round to the forehead, the aim kept on the man; watches the dead man's hand grow claws, watches him stand without hands and speak his name, watches the bullet drop out of his head and the hole close — with contempt, not awe. Names the monster an animal, empties the gun into it with relish; the slide locks; he looks at the dead pistol — the one crack — winds up and heaves it like a heavy stone, from behind the back, straight into the face. Human to the last frame.
VICTOR: the host of Part A with the mask off; the anger never resets. Shouts his claim, finger trembling with rage, walks his chest into the barrel. Shot in the head, drops onto the center of the sofa and lies motionless — then the hand changes while he lies there, silent; he rises without hands and speaks on the way up, amused, the boy's name at the end like a hand on his shoulder; lets the bullet drop out of his forehead like a coin he has finished looking at; regrows the flesh of the hole, from the inside, while he makes the offer. Finishes the offer with the head of @char_victor_werewolf_image_v1; takes five bullets like a wall; takes the pistol in the face, shakes it off, roars, loads, charges and dives over the table to tackle Adam to the floor: you will not stand beside me, so you will lie under me. No fear in any second.

ACTING TASKS
THE EVENT (read backward from the ending — the double-meaning last line "I'm allergic to dogs.", said about dogs, meant: my body rejects yours; the last beat the tackle: stand beside me or lie under me): THE CLAIM MADE FLESH — the argument of Part A passes into the two bodies. Victor's body makes the claim: takes a bullet in the head, lies dead, grows claws, stands without hands and talks, drops the bullet out of its own forehead and closes the hole, shows the true face, takes five more bullets — nothing you have works on me, because we are the same kind. Adam's body makes the refusal: no step back, no raised voice, the gun kept on the dead man, and when the gun is empty, the gun itself thrown. Both live inside this one event; neither plays the theme.
CONTRAST PAIR (axis: does Kenny's death weigh anything): VICTOR — the claim, the kinship, the true self set free (+) / Kenny weighs nothing, the anger is about himself (−); his anger is scar tissue over the need to be chosen by his own kind. ADAM — no words left, only lead and a thrown pistol (−) / the dead friend steers every quiet word and every pull of the trigger (+); his calm is what loyalty looks like tonight.
CHANNELS: VICTOR through the BODY — the fall, the stillness, the hand, the rise with the voice, the bullet dropped from the forehead, the skin closing, the face finished behind Adam's back, five bullets shrugged off. ADAM through the WEAPON — the finger onto the trigger, the one round, the aim held, the five rounds, the empty slide, the throw.
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): carry it to the end without giving up a step — nobody runs, calls or begs; the only backward movement is what the hits drive into a body. The horror is that nobody plays fear.
ADAM — MOTIVE: Kenny steers every word and every pull; the thing across the table is what he refuses to become. GOAL: end it — one round; when it is not done, finish the refusal with the magazine, then with the gun itself. OBSTACLE: the dead man's hand grows claws, the dead man stands without hands and says his name, drops the bullet out of his own head and closes the hole; five rounds do nothing; one step back or one raised voice hands Victor the boy he is fishing for. TACTIC: refuse through the weapon — read both of Victor's eyes after every move; after the head shot read the body for the trick and keep the gun on it; watch the change as a trick that changes nothing; pronounce the sentence and fire it; when the gun locks open, spend the gun.
Moment to moment — B1: take the finger and the half-step as the last thing he allows; tighten the grip, finger onto the trigger. "Shut your mouth.": shut the door on the conversation; let the pistol finish the sentence. The one shot: spend one round as the last word — the head, where the talking comes from; watch it land. The still body and the claws (offscreen): read the body for the trick, keep the gun on it. Under the rise and "…Adam." (offscreen): hear his own name in that mouth and lock the jaw; hold the aim on the man who should be dead. Under the bullet and the healing (offscreen, then back to camera): decide it changes nothing; listen for the voice changing and refuse to turn; not a degree of the shoulders. The held silence: make the monster wait. "I'm allergic to dogs.": name the thing an animal and watch the word land — a verdict read to the condemned. Five shots: as fast as the trigger goes, with relish, eyes on him between flashes; hear five pings come back and feel the slide lock. The look at the pistol: the one crack — check it as if it could answer where the rest went; half a breath; take the anger back into the hand and wind up. The throw: put the whole body into the heave — the gun is heavy — and drive it flat into the face; follow it with the eyes. Under the roar and the charge: refuse the roar a flinch; watch the weight come — two steps and the dive — and keep looking at it; no step back. (Safety: gaze always working on Victor, never glassy; natural blink cadence outside held beats.)
VICTOR — MOTIVE: one of his own kind kneels to humans and would rather put a bullet in his head than take his hand; the anger of Part A only finds a bigger body. GOAL: make the boy stand beside him; failing that, lay him under him. OBSTACLE: the round in the head is the plainest refusal; the sentence through bared teeth is the last door; the object in his face is the insult the offer cannot survive. TACTIC: argue through the body — give the boy his dead man, take it back with the hand, then the rise and the voice, then drop his bullet out of his forehead at his feet and close the hole while making the offer; finish the offer monster; take five more rounds as nothing; when the object hits the face, stop asking.
Moment to moment — B1: SHOUT the claim over the gun, hammer it with the finger, walk the chest into the barrel: shoot, then; on "Always were." check both his eyes. Under "Shut your mouth.": drive the finger in harder. The head shot: take it, land in the middle of the sofa, let go completely. The stillness: give the boy everything he came for — nothing moves, nothing breathes. The hand: take the dead man back with the fingers first, in silence. The rise and "…fun at all, Adam.": up out of death without touching the sofa, arching through the back, head last — and speak on the way up, low and amused, the name at the end like a hand on his shoulder; from the top look at the boy and do not step: let him come. The bullet: let the round drop out of the forehead like a coin he has finished looking at — eyes on Adam, not on the bullet; leave the hole open for him to see. "We should be on the same side." (human, the hole knitting shut): reproach — he has just put a round in the head of the only one who understands him — and let the boy watch the flesh grow back together while he says it; the point makes itself; hunt his back for a turn. Behind Adam's back: finish becoming what he is, unseen. "You and me." (as he comes into view): the claim with the true face, no more courtesy; hold the silence. Under "I'm allergic to dogs." and the five shots (offscreen): the final refusal; stand through the rounds like a wall. The pistol in the face: the hit is nothing, the meaning everything — shake it off, let every offer die. The roar, the charge and the tackle: stop asking; gather the weight, go at the boy and nothing else, and put him on the floor. (Safety: gaze engaged, never glassy; the one exception the motionless stretch at 5.5–7.4s — the deliberate picture of a switched-off body.)

ACTION TIMING
0.0–2.6s — SHOT 1 — EXTREME-WIDE HIGH THREE-QUARTER MASTER (FIRST AXIS). The frame of FIRST FRAME exactly: the whole room from the high corner at 45 degrees, both men full figure and small, Adam left nearer, Victor right farther in front of the entire sofa wall, the table between them. 0.0–0.4s: the duel of eyes. 0.4–2.2s — VICTOR, B1, SHOUTED, hammering each word with the trembling finger, a HALF STEP forward chest-first into the barrel: "You're one of us, kid. Always were." 2.2–2.6s: Adam's answer is one centimetre — knuckles whiten, the aim pushes forward, the index finger slides onto the trigger.
HARD CUT.
2.6–4.6s — SHOT 2 — CLOSE ON ADAM, PULLING BACK TO THE PISTOL; ONE SHOT (FIRST AXIS). CLOSE-UP on Adam's face from the bar side, his right front, 0.8 metres, eye height, canted 6–10 degrees; Adam left-center, three-quarter, eyes screen-right; the pistol not yet in frame. 2.6–2.8s: the face has decided. 2.8–3.5s — ADAM, B2, low, through bared human teeth: "Shut your mouth." 3.5–4.0s: on the last word the camera PULLS BACK and a little down into a MEDIUM, bringing his extended right arm and the pistol — level, pointing screen-right — into the right part of the frame; the face sharp left-center. 4.2s: ONE SHOT — one full, emphatic pull, the whole arm committing, recoil kicking the wrist up, one muzzle flash on the side of his face, the barrel back on the line; the human ringed hand of @char_adam_video_v1. 4.2–4.6s: eyes on Victor, snarl held, pistol level.
HARD CUT.
4.6–7.4s — SHOT 3 — ON VICTOR: THE HEAD SHOT, THE FALL, MOTIONLESS (FIRST AXIS). Camera on Adam's side of the table, chest height: a MEDIUM on Victor in the RIGHT part of the frame in front of the red sofa, three-quarter profile facing screen-left; sofa and painting behind him. Handheld, lively. 4.6–4.7s: the bullet hits the EXACT CENTER of the forehead — the head SNAPS back — and stops there: the small dark round puncture of @char_victor_wound_image_v1, no wider than his eyebrow, a dry dark dot, exactly where and exactly as big as that reference shows it. 4.7–5.5s: the body goes — he drops backward onto the CENTER of the sofa seat, lands on his backside, slumps into the backrest beneath the painting, the head falls back face to the ceiling, the dark dot in the lamp light, arms flopping out along the seat palms-down, legs splayed, cushions compressing. 5.5–7.4s: MOTIONLESS — no movement, no breath, eyes half-open and unfocused; the dot in the center of the forehead the only mark on him — the head of @char_victor_wound_image_v1. Nobody speaks. END STATE: Victor slumped at the sofa's center, head back, arms out, human head, the hole of @char_victor_wound_image_v1; Adam offscreen, pistol level.
HARD CUT.
7.4–8.8s — SHOT 4 — CLOSE-UP ON VICTOR'S RIGHT HAND, PUSHING IN: THE CLAWS, SILENT (FIRST AXIS). A CLOSE-UP of VICTOR'S right hand palm-down on the red leather of the seat where it fell — the hand in the black suit sleeve, no rings, no pistol in this frame; camera low over the cushion from Adam's side, canted, pushing in smoothly the whole shot. Victor's face above the frame, offscreen; Adam offscreen, his hands not in this frame and unchanged. No dialogue in this shot. 7.4–7.6s: the fingers twitch and press flat into the leather. 7.6–8.4s: in one fast surge the fingers LENGTHEN with a crack of knuckles, the skin darkens, dark claws push out from the fingertips — the hand of @char_victor_werewolf_image_v1 — and dig into the leather; sleeve and cuff intact. 8.4–8.8s: the clawed hand presses once into the leather and goes still; the push-in ends tight on it.
HARD CUT.
8.8–14.6s — SHOT 5 — ONE UNBROKEN TAKE, VICTOR FULL FIGURE: THE RISE THROUGH THE BRIDGE FROM LOW AND FROM THE SIDE; THE LINE ON THE WAY UP; AS HE STRAIGHTENS THE BULLET IS PUSHED OUT OF THE FOREHEAD AND FALLS TO THE FLOOR LIKE A GRAIN, THE HOLE STAYS (FIRST AXIS). ONE camera position, ONE continuous take, no cut inside it: the camera about 40 centimetres off the floor on the bar side, well off the sofa's near arm at a three-quarter angle, a wide lens (about 84 degrees) tilted slightly up, framed so that Victor is seen FULL FIGURE from head to shoes in every frame of the shot — seated and standing — with air above his standing head and the floor at his shoes inside the frame; the WHOLE red sofa and the painting above it in frame; the arch of the back reading in near-profile against the wall; canted a few degrees; handheld, static. Everything in this shot — the rise, the line, the bullet leaving the forehead on the straightening and reaching the floor — happens in this one frame, on this one plane, without a cut. First frame: Victor sprawled on the center of the seat, head thrown back, legs spread, arms along the seat, clawed hands open, facing screen-LEFT toward the offscreen Adam. 8.8–9.2s: the hands come off the leather and the arms fall loose; the chest lifts once. 9.2–11.2s — VICTOR, B3, low and amused, a growl under it, spoken AS THE BODY COMES UP through the bridge: "If it were that easy, it wouldn't be any fun at all, Adam." 9.2–11.6s: THE BRIDGE — hips drive up and forward, the spine ARCHES BACKWARD into a bow, chest to the ceiling, head still thrown back, and in that arc the whole body comes up off the seat onto his feet — no hands, the arms hanging loose, never touching the cushions or the sofa arms — acrobatic, UNNATURAL, as if lifted from inside. 11.6–12.6s: he STRAIGHTENS — the spine unrolling from the pelvis upward, the head coming up LAST — and AS THE HEAD COMES LEVEL THE BULLET IS PUSHED OUT OF THE FOREHEAD, in the same unbroken frame, out of the hole in the CENTER OF HIS FOREHEAD and from nowhere else: the skin around the dot tightens with the effort of the straightening; the bullet of @prop_spent_bullet — a micro grain smaller than the hole, 3–4 millimetres, the size of a grain of rice, identical in shape, material and colour to the photo — is squeezed out of the forehead dot BASE FIRST — copper cylinder first, grey-lead petals following, stretching the small hole for an instant — stands proud of the forehead for a frame, tilts over the lower rim and FALLS straight down in front of him, a tiny dark grain dropping from the forehead, the fall followed all the way to the FLOOR, where it lands at his shoes inside the frame like a dropped grain; his chest and jacket stay untouched — nothing comes out of them; his eyes stay on Adam, never on the bullet. He is upright by 12.6s: in front of the sofa's center, arms straight down, clawed hands open, fingers spread, shoulders rolled forward, eyes on the offscreen Adam; human head, the HOLE STAYS — a dark empty dot in the center of the forehead. 12.6–14.6s: he stands ON THE SPOT, not one step toward Adam, the dark dot in his forehead, the eyes on him. END STATE: standing full figure in front of the sofa's center, human head, the open hole of @char_victor_wound_image_v1 in the forehead, the bullet of @prop_spent_bullet on the floor at his shoes in frame, clawed hands open; one take, no cut.
HARD CUT.
